title: Principles ten to thirteen
hookLine: God knows, rewards and punishes, the messiah will come, the dead will live

cards: Thirteen lines, and every one opens the same way. I believe with complete faith. That's the shape of a version of Maimonides' list printed in prayer books, set out after the morning service.

It isn't his own wording. Someone later recast each foundation as a sentence a person could say in the first person, out loud. So the list stops being a page of philosophy and becomes something said with the mouth.
Today, the last four lines, the ones that look ahead.

teach.b: Principles ten to thirteen. The tenth: God knows what human beings do and think. Not in a general way, from far off.
The Psalms say God fashions the hearts of all people and considers all their deeds. Nothing a person does falls outside God's notice.
The eleventh: God rewards those who keep the commandments and punishes those who break them.
Maimonides holds that the final reward is the world to come, the share this whole list began with.

teach.h: WAITING FOR THE MESSIAH, EVERY DAY.
teach.b: The twelfth: the messiah will come. And here the prayer-book version adds a phrase. Even though he may delay, I wait for him every day that he will come.
Not a date on a calendar. A waiting that starts over each morning.

The thirteenth: the dead will live again, at a time God chooses. That's the resurrection of the dead, a belief already present in the Mishnah chapter Maimonides was explaining. Now look at the whole list from here.
It began with God, who has no beginning. It passed through prophecy and the Torah. And it ends with things that haven't happened yet.
A creed that closes on hope rather than on a fact already settled. Some Jews say these lines each morning. Others study them, and argue with them, which is tomorrow.
Each line still opens the same way.

how: Some Jews recite the thirteen "I believe" lines, Ani Ma'amin, after the morning service; the twelfth line, about waiting for the messiah, is also sung to several melodies.

games.q: what does “principles ten to thirteen” mean?
o: four laws about mourning and caring for the dead
the last four: God knows, rewards, and what's still to come
four signs that the end of days has already come

games.q: principles ten to thirteen — tap the pairs.

s: the "I believe" lines are Maimonides' own wording
a later version recast each foundation as a first-person line.
the twelfth line waits for the messiah every day
even though he may delay, the line waits for him each day.
the list ends with God's existence
it begins there, and ends with what hasn't happened yet: the messiah and the dead living again.

games.q: you're recasting Maimonides' list so people can say it aloud. how should each line begin?
games.why: the prayer-book version opens every line with the same first-person words: I believe with complete faith.

practice: Bring to mind one thing you're waiting for, for yourself, for someone you love, or for the world: not a plan, a hope.
The twelfth line waits every day without knowing the day; hold your hope that way for a few breaths, open and unhurried. If you pray, you can hold it before God.

wordCard.voice: Principles ten to thirteen. God knows what people do, God rewards and punishes, the messiah will come, and the dead will live. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: I believe, the words that open each line of the prayer-book version of the list.

carryVoice: Your line: I believe with complete faith. Waiting can start fresh each morning. Until tomorrow.
